UNITED STATES OF AMERICA
                                                 BEFORE THE
                        FEDERAL ENERGY REGULATORY COMMISSION
                                                               )
PJM Interconnection, L.L.C.                                    )                 Docket No. ER26-3380-000
                                                               )


                         MOTION FOR LEAVE TO ANSWER
             AND ANSWER OF CONSTELLATION ENERGY GENERATION, LLC

           Pursuant to Rules 212 and 213 of the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission’s (“FERC”

or the “Commission”) Rules of Practice and Procedure, 1 Constellation Energy Generation, LLC

(“Constellation”) respectfully moves for leave to answer and answers the Motion for Leave to

Answer and Answer of PJM Interconnection, L.L.C. (“PJM”). 2 Constellation seeks to provide

additional information and context that will assist the Commission in its decision-making process. 3

I.         BACKGROUND

           On July 31, 2026, PJM Interconnection, L.L.C. (“PJM”) submitted revisions to the PJM

Open Access Transmission Tariff (“Tariff”) and the Reliability Assurance Agreement Among

Load Serving Entities (“RAA”) to establish the Reliability Backstop Procurement (“RBP”). 4



1
     18 C.F.R. §§ 385.212, 385.213.
2
 PJM Interconnection, L.L.C., Motion for Leave to Answer and Answer of PJM Interconnection, L.L.C., Docket
No. ER26-3380-000 (filed Sept. 10, 2026) (“PJM Answer”).
3
  Although the Commission’s Rules of Practice and Procedure do not generally permit answers to answers unless
otherwise ordered by the decisional authority, the Commission has made exceptions where an answer provides useful
and relevant information that will assist the Commission in its decision-making process, corrects factual inaccuracies
and clarifies the issues, or assures a complete record in the proceeding. See, e.g., Pioneer Transmission, LLC v. N.
Ind. Pub. Serv. Co., 140 FERC ¶ 61,057, at P 94 (2012) (accepting answers that “provided information that assisted
us in our decision-making process”); Entergy Servs., Inc., 126 FERC ¶ 61,227, at P 76, order on clarification & reh’g,
127 FERC ¶ 61,225 (2009); New Power Co. v. PJM Interconnection LLC, 98 FERC ¶ 61,208, at p. 61,756 (2002)
(answer accepted to provide new factual and legal material to assist the Commission in decision-making process).
4
  PJM Interconnection, L.L.C., Reliability Backstop Procurement to Address Resource Adequacy Concerns Stemming
from Large Loads, Docket No. ER26-3380-000 (filed July 31, 2026) (“PJM Proposal”). Capitalized terms used but
not otherwise defined herein have the meaning as defined in the Tariff, the RAA, or the PJM Proposal, as applicable.

                                                          1
 Numerous parties filed comments and protests addressing the proposal, including Constellation.5

In response, PJM filed the PJM Answer on September 10, 2026. The PJM Answer addressed

certain issues raised by Constellation in its Limited Protest and Answer. Constellation submits

this answer to briefly respond to the PJM Answer and provide clarification that will assist the

Commission in its decision in this proceeding.

II.        ANSWER

           A.       Eddystone and Similarly Situated Energy Resources Should Qualify as RBP
                    Resources and Resources Eligible to Supply Qualifying RBP Offset UCAP
                    MW

           On September 11, 2026, the D.C. Circuit issued a unanimous ruling vacating the

Department of Energy’s (“DOE”) order issued under section 202(c) Federal Power Act (“FPA”)

requiring Consumers Energy to continue operating the J.H. Campbell power plant (the “Campbell

Order”). 6 The Campbell Order could have implications for other electric generators currently

operating pursuant to the Secretary’s authority under section 202(c), including Constellation’s

Eddystone Units 3 & 4 (“Eddystone”). The court rejected the DOE’s interpretation of section

202(c), finding that no “emergency” existed to warrant a section 202(c) order. 7 Legal challenges

to other DOE orders under section 202(c), including with respect to Eddystone, remain pending.

In light of this development and its implications, Constellation provides additional clarification

regarding its earlier request to modify the criteria for resources eligible to provide Qualifying RBP

Offset UCAP MW and RBP Sell Offers. 8



5
  See PJM Interconnection, L.L.C., Limited Protest of Constellation Energy Generation, LLC, Docket No. ER26-
3380-000 (filed Aug. 21, 2026) (“Limited Protest”); PJM Interconnection, L.L.C., Motion for Leave to Answer and
Answer of Constellation Energy Generation, LLC, Docket No. ER26-3380-000 (filed Sept. 8, 2026) (“Answer”).
6
    People of the State of Michigan v. U.S. Department of Energy, No. 25-1159 (D.C. Cir. Sept. 11, 2026).
7
    Id.
8
    Limited Protest at 13–14; Answer at 2–3.

                                                           2
            On December 1, 2023, Constellation announced its plans to retire Eddystone. The day

prior to the scheduled deactivation, on May 30, 2025, the Secretary declared that the operational

availability and economic dispatch of Eddystone was necessary to meet an emergency on the

system and directed Constellation to keep the units online. The Secretary has extended its 202(c)

order for Eddystone continuously since, most recently on August 21, 2026. 9 Notably, those DOE

orders direct that the Eddystone units “shall not be considered capacity resources.” 10 As a result,

Constellation requested, and the Commission granted, a request for waiver to remove Eddystone

Units 3 and 4 from Capacity Resource status and transferred the Capacity Interconnection Rights

(“CIRs”) from Eddystone to Crane Clean Energy Center earlier this year. 11 Eddystone is now an

energy-only resource with no capacity rights.

           Once Eddystone is no longer subject to a DOE 202(c) order, it could proceed with

deactivation as planned. Or, if commercially practicable, it could request to become a new capacity

resource. To be clear, from a PJM perspective the path to becoming a new capacity resource for

Eddystone would look no different from that of a new build resource or an uprate to an existing

capacity resource: it would require entry into the interconnection queue and payment to upgrade

the transmission system as necessary.              Network upgrade costs are uncertain but could be

significant—potentially in the tens of millions or even hundreds of millions of dollars.

            While uncertainty remains, Eddystone’s ability to qualify as an RBP Resource and/or

Qualifying RBP Offset UCAP MW could provide a viable economic path forward for keeping its



9
 Dep’t of Energy, Order No. 202-26-40 (Aug. 21, 2026); Dep’t of Energy, Order No. 202-26-24 (May 21, 2026);
Dep’t of Energy, Order No. 202-26-17 (Feb. 23, 2026) (“Feb. 2026 Eddystone Order”); Dep’t of Energy, Order No.
202-25-10 (Nov. 25, 2025); Dep’t of Energy, Order No. 202-25-8 (Aug. 28, 2025); Dep’t of Energy, Order No. 202-
25-4 (May 30, 2025).
10
     Feb. 2026 Eddystone Order at 10, Ordering Para. G (emphasis added).
11
     See Constellation Energy Generation, LLC, 195 FERC ¶ 61,162 (2026).

                                                         3
 units online rather than proceeding with deactivation as planned. The RBP as currently proposed,

however, does not appear to contemplate an admittedly unusual scenario like Eddystone’s: an

energy-only resource that is considering adding new capacity to the grid by acquiring new

Capacity Interconnection Rights and new Installed Capacity. 12

           In the PJM Answer, PJM dismissed Constellation’s requests with little explanation. 13 We

respectfully submit that PJM is overlooking one of the better opportunities to unlock new capacity

quickly. The Eddystone units are already fully permitted and constructed, with fuel supply in place,

and do not face the significant land acquisition, construction, permitting, supply chain and other

issues that new generation inevitably face. Eddystone would need to seek new CIRs through an

Interconnection Request, and, accordingly, bear its share of any required Network Upgrades, but

Eddystone is otherwise uniquely positioned to provide new capacity to the grid.

           Accordingly, Constellation maintains its prior requests for relief with the additional clarity

and context provided herein. As previously discussed, 14 minor changes to the PJM Proposal would

make clear that an energy-only resource obtaining new capacity rights would qualify for RBP

(whether as a RBP Seller or as Qualifying RBP Offset UCAP MW). This clarification to the

eligibility rules would be consistent with the overall framework of PJM’s RBP and PJM’s stated

intent of procuring new capacity to address the region’s capacity shortfall.

           B.       PJM Mischaracterizes the Commission’s Treatment of Price Taker
                    Requirements in Prior Proceedings

           The PJM Answer claimed that the Commission should disregard the concerns raised in

Constellation’s Limited Protest regarding the RBP’s price taker requirement because the


12
     PJM Answer at 41.
13
     Id.
14
     Limited Protest at 13–14; Answer at 2–3.

                                                     4
 Commission has found in other proceedings, particularly in the context of Reliability Must Run

(“RMR”) resources, that offering resources into the PJM Reliability Pricing Model (“RPM”) as

price takers is just and reasonable. 15 This comparison is misguided. The Commission should not

rely on its limited RMR precedent to guide its decision here for the following reasons:

          •   PJM Ignores the Commission’s Balancing Analysis in its RMR Proceeding. In its

              RMR proceedings (and other proceedings considering the impact of price taker offers

              by resources with out-of-market support), the Commission engages in a balancing

              analysis to determine whether it is just and reasonable to require out-of-market

              resources to offer as price takers, wherein it balances market and resource adequacy

              impacts and cost impacts to determine whether a proposal is just and reasonable. 16 This

              balancing analysis is fact specific, and the RMR proceedings considered, among other

              things, the unique nature of RMR units, the nature of the service provided, and the

              magnitude and duration of such service. Here, PJM has not engaged in any meaningful

              balancing that considers the impact of RBP resources offering as price takers on

              markets, resource adequacy or costs, let alone provided evidence that the specific facts

              applicable to RBP resource (including, the uncertainty as to when or if the associated

              load will materialize, the duration and magnitude of the RBP service, etc.) justify

              PJM’s proposed result. As described below, the Commission should find that the

              balancing analysis here, unlike in the RMR proceedings, weighs against finding that

              PJM’s price taker requirement is just and reasonable.



15
     PJM Answer at 47–51.
16
   See, e.g., PJM Interconnection, L.L.C., 192 FERC ¶ 61,135, at P 31 (2025) (acknowledging that “treating RMR
resources as price takers in the capacity market may affect capacity prices,” but finding “on balance” that such
treatment is necessary to avoid customers paying for more capacity than needed).

                                                        5
            •   Load Served by RMR Resources Already Exists. Resources subject to RMR

               agreements are already serving existing load, with such generation operating past

               planned deactivation dates in response to a well-studied transmission reliability

               problem. Such RMR resources continue to operate to ensure transmission reliability

               for existing load until specific and necessary transmission system upgrades are

               completed. On the other hand, the load expected to be served by RBP resources is not

               yet energized, and as explained in Constellation’s Limited Protest and Answer and Dr.

               Shanker’s supporting testimony, 17 there is risk this load may be delayed or never

               energized at all. Others agree this distinction between existing load and new large load

               is a meaningful concern. For example, in PJM’s Interim Resource Adequacy Service

               proceeding, Southern Maryland Electric Cooperative, Inc. explained that new large

               loads “are, as a structural matter, disproportionately likely to be projects still working

               through interconnection, construction, or commissioning, rather than loads already

               drawing their full expected demand, if any demand at all based upon the state of project

               development.” 18 Thus, the impact on markets, resource adequacy provided by existing

               resources, and costs overall could be far greater in the RBP context where there is no

               load certainty than in the RMR context where the load already exists.

           •   The Magnitude of the Initial RBP Target Far Outweighs that Typical of RMR

               Resources. RMR resources in operation in PJM have historically been few in number,




17
     Limited Protest at 8–10, Shanker Aff. ¶¶ 13–17.
18
  PJM Interconnection, L.L.C., Comments and Limited Protest of Southern Maryland and Electric Cooperative,
Inc., Docket No. ER26-3515-000 (filed Sept. 3, 2026); see also PJM Interconnection, L.L.C., Motion for Leave to
Answer and Answer of the New Jersey Board of Public Utilities, Docket No. ER26-3515-000 (filed Sept. 18, 2026)
(expressing concern that “New Large Loads may not be yet energized, or may have only just begun a ramp or testing
period that is below its expected draw”).

                                                       6
                averaging a few hundred MWs at any given time over the past twenty plus years. 19

               Even the all-time high amount of RMRs on the system (i.e., the two RMR resources

               relevant in the proceeding cited by PJM—Brandon Shores Generating Station Units 1

               and 2 and Wagner Generating Station Units 3 and 4) together account for under 2,000

               MW. 20 On the other hand, the volume of RBP capacity (initially targeting 6,831 MWs)

               is expected to be significantly more than these typical RMR volumes, including three

               times the peak RMR volume considered in the cited PJM RMR proceeding. The impact

               of this volume of RBP capacity on market signals, resource adequacy and ultimately

               costs in the RPM will be far greater than was ever considered in the RMR proceeding.

           •   RMR Resources Offer As Price Takers for a Relatively Short, Time-Limited

               Period. The time period during which RMR resources act as price takers is generally

               more limited to cover only the brief period of time necessary to address short-term

               transmission reliability needs, typically under three years. 21             Indeed, the RMR

               resources referenced in the RMR proceeding PJM cites are expected to serve as RMR

               resources for only a few delivery years. 22 In fact, the Commission “has emphasized

               that RMR agreements should be of a limited duration so as to not perpetuate out-of-

               market solutions that have the potential, if not undertaken in an open and transparent

               manner, to undermine price formation.” 23 In contrast, RBP resources will offer as

                 price takers in each RPM for up to 15 years—again resulting in outsized impact on

                markets, resource adequacy and costs—a duration far greater than what was

                contemplated in the RMR proceedings.

           •    The Commission Must Consider the Cumulative Effect of PJM’s Out-of-Market

                Interventions. Like the RBP, the RMR proposal cited by PJM was an “interim,” “stop-

                gap” solution “while PJM work[ed] with stakeholders to develop a more fulsome

                proposal.” 24     Since then, PJM has also enacted other significant out-of-market,

                “interim” measures, including price caps and the RBP itself, that affect RPM price

                signals.    But these cumulative impacts were not considered in the cases cited by PJM

                or any analysis it provided. Rather, as discussed in Constellation’s Limited Protest,

                PJM itself recognizes what it calls the “credibility trap,” where “high scarcity prices

                that are economically necessary to signal the need for investment become, in this

                environment, the trigger for governmental intervention that undermines the credibility

                of those same prices . . . . Investors, anticipating further intervention, discount the

                durability of the price signal. Capital stays on the sidelines; the shortage persists.” 25 In

                its balancing analysis, the Commission must consider the cumulative effect of PJM’s

                repeated out-of-market interventions and the long-term impact and find that this aspect

                of PJM’s proposal is not just and reasonable.


Producers of N.Y. v. N.Y. Indep. Sys. Operator, Inc., 150 FERC ¶ 61,214, at P 69 (2015), order on reh’g &
clarification, 170 FERC ¶ 61,118 (2020) (“Unlike the RSSA contracts discussed in the original Complaint that
procure adequate capacity to address short-term reliability needs, the Dunkirk repowering agreement appears to

if the additional capacity created by the repowering agreement above the amount needed for short-term reliability is
allowed to offer into the NYISO capacity market at prices below the cost of repowering, such capacity might deter
new entry or displace less-costly existing capacity in NYCA. As a result, capacity market prices could be artificially
suppressed.”).

25

            C.      Constellation Supports PJM’s Suggestion to Sever Credit and Collateral
                   Issues

           Constellation and others raised concerns about the load serving entity (“LSE”) collateral

and credit requirements in the PJM Proposal. 26 In the PJM Answer, PJM acknowledged that

“reasonable minds may differ on the credit approach,” and “consent[ed] to the Commission

resolving the applicable buyer-side LSE RBP Credit Rate through additional procedures.” 27 Given

the complexity and enormity of the potential LSE credit requirements, and given that “the LSE

credit rules do not need to be effective for the RBP to be conducted,” 28 Constellation appreciates

PJM’s openness on these issues and supports, as described in its Answer, severing these credit

issues and establishing an expedited paper hearing limited to proposed Tariff section 18.8(b). 29

 III.    CONCLUSION

        In accordance with PJM’s willingness to accept changes under NRG Power Marketing, 30

the Commission should (i) accept the RBP subject to the modifications Constellation discussed in

its Limited Protest and Answer, as clarified herein, and (ii) sever the LSE credit issue discussed in

its Answer for further proceedings and refer that issue to an expedited paper hearing.
